title: What if all copper disappeared for 5 seconds?
description:
What if every bit of copper on Earth vanished for just 5 seconds? New York goes dark, Lady Liberty loses her skin, and every penny turns gray. The lights don't come back when the copper does.

Sources: USGS (copper uses, car wiring), National Park Service (Statue of Liberty), U.S. Mint via Live Science (pennies), CBS News / Con Edison (2003 blackout).

title: 5 lightning "facts." Only one is true.
description:
Only one of these 5 lightning "facts" is true. Can you guess which before the reveal?

Four are myths: the same place twice, rubber tires, no rain overhead and "heat lightning." Stay for the bonus: the 5-second count that tells you how far away a storm is.

Sources: National Weather Service (How Hot Is Lightning?; Understanding Lightning: Thunder; NWS Fort Worth Myths vs. Facts), MPR News and Live Science (Empire State Building strikes).

title: If the Sun were a door, where's Earth?
description:
If the Sun were as tall as your front door, where would Earth be?

NASA says Earth would be the size of a nickel. Shrink everything else to match and Earth sits 215 meters down the street, Neptune 6.5 km away, and the nearest star 57,600 km away: 1.4 times around the whole planet.

Sources: NASA Science (Earth facts, Sun facts, Neptune facts), NASA Space Place (How Big is the Sun?). Distances are scale math from NASA figures.

title: Why does your watch count to 32,768?
description:
Why does your watch count to 32,768?

Most quartz watches hide a tiny quartz tuning fork that vibrates 32,768 times a second, and the chip halves that 15 times to make exactly 1 tick per second. But the second itself is defined by cesium atoms, and NIST says its NIST-F4 clock, had it started 100 million years ago, would be off by less than a second today.

Sources: NIST (Timekeeping and clocks FAQs; NIST-F4 news release, April 2025), Live Science (Why is Quartz Used in Watches?). Halving math: 32,768 = 2^15.

title: What if you poured Hoover Dam all at once?
description:
What if Hoover Dam had been poured in one giant go?

Reclamation's engineers calculated the concrete would get so hot it would take 125 years to cool, and the stress would crack it apart. So they built it as columns, 5 feet at a time, with more than 582 miles of steel cooling pipe. All that heat could have baked 500,000 loaves of bread a day for 3 years.

Sources: U.S. Bureau of Reclamation (Hoover Dam: Concrete essay; Hoover Dam FAQs). 1933 + 125 years and 500,000 × 365 × 3 are simple math.

title: Where's the coldest place in the universe? (#1 is man-made)
description:
Where's the coldest place in the universe? #1 isn't natural at all.

We ranked 5 of the coldest places we know: Antarctica's record −89.2 °C, Pluto, the Big Bang's afterglow, the Boomerang Nebula, and a box on the space station where lasers chill atoms to about a ten-billionth of a degree above absolute zero.

Sources: World Meteorological Organization; NASA (Pluto Facts, Cold Atom Laboratory, Space Station Facts and Figures); NASA/JPL (The Coolest Experiment in the Universe); ESA/Hubble (Boomerang Nebula); NIST (absolute zero = −273.15 °C). −273.1499999999 °C is math: −273.15 °C plus one ten-billionth of a degree.
